title: Government says a third of absent Year 10‑11 pupils end up not in education, employment or training
content: The government estimates that about one‑third of persistently absent Year 10 and 11 pupils in England eventually leave education, employment and training.
summary: The government believes around a third of young people who are persistently absent in Years 10 and 11 in England go on to be not in education, employment or training. The government estimates this proportion is about one third.
author: BBC Politics

title: COP31 draft climate deal urges faster shift from fossil fuels
content:
COP31 has released a draft of the cover decision that ties together the summit’s outcomes, and the text calls for a faster shift away from fossil fuels. The draft is now being examined by diplomats, journalists, activists and scientists.

During a press conference, Australia’s climate minister Chris Bowen, who is also president of the negotiations, said it “is a given” that parties will not reach agreement on every element of the draft. He noted that the timing of this COP, alongside the rise of artificial intelligence, war and cost‑of‑living crises, makes it important to demonstrate that multilateralism works, adding that the world wants action on climate change amid a “polycrisis.”

Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley described the “cancer of indifference” to the climate crisis as pushing the world closer to the brink. Further expert analysis of the draft will follow.
summary: A draft cover decision released at COP31 calls for a faster shift away from fossil fuels. Australia’s climate minister Chris Bowen said parties will not agree on all elements of the draft, and Mia Mottley warned that indifference to the climate crisis is pushing the world toward the brink.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Cop31 draft text aims to draw out parties, says Australia’s talks president
content: Many countries surprised to see first version delivered with more than four days of negotiation remaining A draft text of a possible final outcome from the Cop31 UN climate summit is an attempt to “draw out parties” on their areas of agreement and disagreement, Australia’s president of the talks has said. Many countries were surprised to see a first draft of a potential “cover decision” from the fortnight-long talks early on Monday afternoon, with more than four days of negotiation still to go. The text includes several proposals regarded as highly contentious by some countries, including a call to “immediately transition away from fossil fuels”.
summary: The president of the Cop31 talks, Australia’s president of the talks, said the draft text is meant to “draw out parties” on areas of agreement and disagreement. The draft, released early with more than four days of negotiation remaining, includes contentious proposals such as an immediate transition away from fossil fuels, surprising many countries.
author: Guardian Environment

title: EPA’s Aspect chemical-detection plane grounded during Oklahoma leak, Texas fire, Ohio blasts
content:
The EPA’s Aspect chemical-detection plane, once a critical tool for monitoring toxic substances during disasters, has frequently remained grounded in recent years. The aircraft did not deploy during an ammonia leak in Weatherford, Oklahoma, that injured 74 people last November, nor during a March fire at a Valero refinery in Port Arthur, Texas, or August blasts at a recycling plant in Toledo, Ohio, which killed two workers.

Mark Thomas, a former EPA official who managed the program for 18 years, noted that the plane would have responded to all these incidents a decade ago. The article highlights this decline in operational readiness while also inviting readers to submit climate questions for upcoming Stateside guest Bill McKibben.
summary: EPA’s Aspect chemical-detection plane grounded during Oklahoma leak, Texas fire, Ohio blasts.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Cape Cod harvester Ernie Eldredge finds non‑native clam, signaling invasion
content:
Shellfish harvester Ernie Eldredge was working ankle‑deep in the tidal flats of Chatham, Massachusetts, on Cape Cod when he encountered an unfamiliar clam in a 2023 harvest. After pulling his rake through fine white sand without hearing the usual “clink” of shells, Eldredge set the specimen aside and consulted a scientist for identification. Together they determined that the mollusk was a potentially harmful, non‑native species, marking what Eldredge described as the start of an invasion.

Eldredge noted that the tidal flats on the elbow of Cape Cod are constantly shifting, with recent fall winds bringing additional sand into the area. He observed that the clams he had been finding over the summer may have moved on, prompting his continued search across the changing landscape.
summary: Shellfish harvester Ernie Eldredge discovered an unfamiliar mollusk in his 2023 haul on Cape Cod’s tidal flats in Chatham, Massachusetts. He consulted a scientist who identified it as a potentially harmful non‑native species, indicating the start of an invasion.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Al Gore says passing Baaja bill to speed gas projects and datacenters would be mistake
content: Former US vice-president at Cop31 urges lawmakers to rethink contentious bipartisan Baaja bill advanced by the US Senate It would be a “serious mistake” to pass a contentious bipartisan bill to speed up energy projects and datacenters that has divided Democrats and environmentalists, Al Gore said. The legislation, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (Baaja), will make it easier to build large infrastructure projects in the US, from oil and gas pipelines and datacenters to crucial clean energy components such as solar and wind power and transmission lines, scaling back environmental protections and legal challenges in order to do so.
summary: Al Gore, former US vice‑president, urged lawmakers to reconsider the bipartisan Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (Baaja) advanced by the Senate. He said the bill would scale back environmental protections and legal challenges while easing construction of oil and gas pipelines, datacenters, and clean‑energy infrastructure.
author: Guardian Environment

title: US hyperscaler datacenters emit CO2 equal to Denmark's yearly output, study says
content:
A new study reports that the rapid expansion of “hyperscaler” data centers in the United States has generated carbon‑dioxide emissions comparable to Denmark’s total annual output. The research attributes the emissions to the facilities’ reliance on dirtier power sources to satisfy their large energy demands.

During the period examined, 403 hyperscaler data centers—identified as the largest facilities primarily supporting artificial‑intelligence growth—produced roughly 25.7 million metric tons of CO₂, matching the scale of Denmark’s yearly emissions.
summary: The buildout of 403 hyperscaler datacenters in the United States emitted about 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide. That amount of emissions is roughly equivalent to Denmark’s total annual emissions, according to the study.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Large wave knocks down beachgoer in northern California on Nov. 14
content: A large wave knocked down at least one onlooker on a northern California beach on 14 November as heavy tides battered the West Coast over the weekend. Waves along the coastline reached up to 50 feet, driven by swells intensified by El Niño that slammed into seaside communities.
summary: A large wave knocked down at least one onlooker on a beach in northern California on 14 November. Waves reached up to 50 ft as heavy tides and El Niño‑enhanced swells battered the west coast over the weekend.
author: Guardian Environment

title: 75 native-born olive ridley hatchlings released in California after first recorded nests
content:
Two months after the discovery of the first sea‑turtle nests ever recorded on the U.S. West Coast, the eggs have hatched and California’s first group of 75 native‑born olive ridley turtles have been released into the Pacific Ocean. The nests, found in September on southern California beaches, were incubated at the Aquarium of the Pacific in Long Beach.

The historic nesting, identified in two separate sites, is attributed to a shift likely driven by this year’s El Niño conditions, prompting the unprecedented release of the hatchlings.
summary: 75 native-born olive ridley hatchlings released in California after first recorded nests.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Researchers identify possible method to shield brain from HIV and opioid damage
content: Researchers have identified a potential method to protect the brain from damage linked to HIV infection and opioid use. People living with HIV often experience memory loss, difficulty concentrating and impaired decision‑making, and these cognitive problems are reported to be more severe in patients who also use opioids, a relationship whose underlying cause had not been understood.
summary: People living with HIV experience memory loss, difficulty concentrating and poor decision‑making even with antiretroviral therapy. Cognitive problems are even more severe in patients who also use opioids, and scientists have not previously understood why.
author: Medical Xpress

title: United States to lose measles-free status amid spreading outbreak
content: This week the United States will lose its designation as a country where measles has been eliminated. The change follows a continuing outbreak of the highly contagious disease, which officials say is spreading across the nation.
summary: The United States will lose its designation as a country where measles has been eliminated this week. The loss follows a spreading outbreak of the highly contagious disease.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Wake Forest researcher finds chicken brain cells survive without oxygen
content: A Wake Forest University researcher, Lara do Amaral‑Silva, reports that chicken brain cells can remain viable without oxygen, challenging the usual expectation that brain cells die within minutes when deprived of oxygen. The finding suggests that chicken brain tissue may survive longer under anoxic conditions.
summary: Brain cells normally die within minutes when deprived of oxygen. Wake Forest University researcher Lara do Amaral‑Silva found that chicken brain cells can survive without oxygen.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Study finds delay and 40% denial rate for pediatric biologic prescriptions
content: A study presented at the American College of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology’s annual meeting in Phoenix (Nov. 12‑16) found a considerable delay between prescribing biologic therapy for pediatric patients and receiving final approval. The study also reported that nearly 40% of prescriptions requiring prior authorization were denied.
summary: A study presented at the American College of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology annual meeting in Phoenix reported a considerable delay from prescription to final approval for pediatric biologic therapy. The study also found that almost 40% of prescriptions requiring prior authorization were denied.
author: Medical Xpress

title: ABIM study: gaps in knowledge linked to 52.3% of California physician disciplinary actions
content: A new American Board of Internal Medicine study published in the Journal of Continuing Education in the Health Professions examined physician disciplinary actions in California and found that gaps in medical knowledge were involved in 52.3% of the cases. The gaps included prescribing inappropriate medications, incorrectly interpreting imaging studies or ordering unnecessary high‑risk procedures.
summary: Gaps in medical knowledge, such as prescribing inappropriate medications, incorrectly interpreting imaging studies or ordering an unnecessary high‑risk procedure, were involved in 52.3% of the physician disciplinary actions reviewed. The findings come from a new American Board of Internal Medicine (ABIM) study published in the Journal of Continuing Education in the Health Professions.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Dartmouth study finds “pink noise” can improve conversation enjoyment
content: Dartmouth researchers have identified a conversational technique they term “pink noise” that could restore more enjoyable and engaging dialogue. Their findings, detailed in a new study published in Science Advances, suggest the approach may help reduce conflict in online exchanges and politically charged family gatherings.
summary: Dartmouth researchers have identified a conversational recipe called “pink noise” that may help people return to more enjoyable and engaging interactions. The findings were reported in a new study published in Science Advances.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Genetic “dimmer switch” may lessen severity in rare muscular dystrophy
content: Two siblings inherited the same rare form of muscular dystrophy that progressively weakens the muscles of the face, shoulders and limbs. Both carried the identical disease‑causing genetic change, yet their clinical courses diverged sharply. The brother first noticed weakness in his early teens and by his 50s could barely walk. In contrast, the sister remained symptom‑free into her late 30s and experienced only mild effects throughout her life.
summary: Two siblings inherited the same rare muscular dystrophy that weakens the face, shoulders and limbs. The brother began noticing weakness in his early teens and could barely walk by his 50s, while the sister remained symptom‑free into her late 30s and was only mildly affected.
author: Medical Xpress

title: England and Wales to wipe criminal records of women convicted of illegal abortions
content: Women who have been arrested or convicted for illegal abortions will have their criminal records erased under new automatic pardons now being implemented in England and Wales. The policy specifically targets women’s records related to abortion offences.
summary: Women arrested or convicted for having illegal abortions will have their criminal records wiped. This will happen as new automatic pardons come into force in England and Wales.
author: BBC Health

title: JPMorgan Chase reports temporary software bug affecting consumer banking
content: JPMorgan Chase has reported that a temporary software bug is affecting its consumer banking services. CNBC’s Eamon Javers noted that there is no indication of malicious actors behind the issue and no evidence that the bug is impacting other banks simultaneously.
summary: JPMorgan Chase says a temporary software bug is affecting its consumer banking. CNBC's Eamon Javers reported there is no indication of bad actors or that the bug is impacting multiple banks.
author: CNBC Business

title: Robert Pattinson named new James Bond as franchise remains multibillion‑pound
content: Big-screen debut of Ian Fleming’s creation in 1962, with Sean Connery as lead in Dr No, was start of marketing dream New James Bond announced... And the name’s Pattinson, Robert Pattinson Share your thoughts on the casting Peter Bradshaw’s take Robert Pattinson’s journey to James Bond James Bond may be 73 years old but the superspy holds a licence to print money, at the centre of an evergreen multibillion-pound franchise spanning blockbuster films, merchandise, licensing deals and sponsorship. The announcement that the Twilight and Batman actor Robert Pattinson is the next Bond comes seven years after Daniel Craig revealed that No Time To Die would be his last outing as 007.
summary: Robert Pattinson named new James Bond as franchise remains multibillion‑pound.
author: Guardian Business

title: Online outages hit Bank of America, Chase, US Bank, Wells Fargo, Truist and Zelle
content:
Customers reported service outages and difficulty accessing online accounts at several major U.S. banks—including Bank of America, Chase, U.S. Bank, Wells Fargo and Truist—as well as the money‑transfer service Zelle on Monday. The disruptions followed a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase that produced ripple effects throughout the financial system.

Chase stated the technical problems were not a systemic issue and were not caused by a cyber‑attack, and said it was working to restore banking services.
summary: Users reported service outages and difficulty accessing online accounts at several major US banks and Zelle on Monday after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects. Chase said the problems were not systemic, not a cyber‑attack, and it is working to restore services.
author: Guardian Business

title: ProPublica finds at least nine firms using Trump tariff refunds for bonuses
content:
ProPublica’s investigation found that at least nine companies receiving refunds for tariffs imposed under the Trump administration are allocating part of those funds to corporate bonuses rather than passing the money back to consumers. The nonprofit news outlet identified the practice by reviewing securities filings and earnings‑call transcripts, which disclosed that the firms are directing some of the tariff refunds to their leadership.

The report highlights a pattern in which the refunded amounts, originally intended to offset costs from the tariffs, are being used to reward executives instead of providing consumer reimbursements. No specific companies were named in the findings.
summary: ProPublica identified at least nine companies that received refunds for paying Donald Trump’s tariffs and are directing some of those funds to corporate leadership. The firms are using the refunds for corporate bonuses instead of reimbursing consumers, according to securities filings and earnings calls.
author: Guardian Business

title: Former minister Alan Milburn proposes gradual cut to NI on under‑25 workers
content: National Insurance (NI) paid by firms on under-25s should be gradually lowered to help create more jobs, according to a new report from former government minister Alan Milburn, due to be published on Tuesday.
summary: A new report by former government minister Alan Milburn will be published on Tuesday. The report recommends that firms’ National Insurance contributions for workers under 25 be gradually lowered to help create more jobs.
author: BBC Business

title: Study Finds Humidity Impacts Durability of Biodegradable Thermoplastic Polymers
content:
A long‑term study has examined how humidity influences the durability of biodegradable thermoplastic polymers.  

Demand for sustainable alternatives to conventional plastics is growing, and biodegradable polymers such as poly(lactic acid) (PLA) are attracting attention for packaging and consumer‑product applications.
summary: A long-term study examined how humidity influences the durability of biodegradable thermoplastic polymers. The research notes growing interest in biodegradable polymers such as poly(lactic acid) for packaging and consumer products.

title: Euclid releases first H‑alpha map of star formation covering 1,900 sq deg
content: Euclid’s H‑alpha observations are being used to map the locations of star formation in distant galaxies. The space telescope, launched in July 2023 to investigate dark matter and dark energy, has now issued its first major data release. The release includes visible and near‑infrared measurements covering roughly 1,900 square degrees—about 14 % of the area planned for the six‑year mission and 5 % of the entire sky—providing an unprecedented dataset for these studies.
summary: Euclid was launched into space in July 2023 to explore dark matter and dark energy. Its first major data release provides visible and near‑infrared observations of about 1,900 square degrees, roughly 14% of the planned area and 5% of the sky.
author: Phys.org

title: Researchers test agrivoltaics to help farmers adapt to hotter, drier conditions
content: Researchers are testing agrivoltaics as a potential tool for farmers facing hotter, drier conditions. In UC Davis’ agricultural research fields, Majdi Abou Najm stood amid a tomato crop under the summer sun, noting that the early‑morning heat was already intense enough to risk scalding tomatoes on the vine.
summary: Researchers are testing agrivoltaics as a method for farmers to cope with hotter, drier conditions. Majdi Abou Najm stood in a tomato crop under the summer sun at UC Davis, noting the heat could scald the tomatoes.
author: Phys.org

title: UCLA nanovial technology traps cells and secretions, advancing bioscience experiments
content: UCLA researchers have created a cellular‑scale test‑tube technology—nanovials that cap and trap individual cells along with their secreted molecules for analysis. The platform has been credited with recent biomedical discoveries, including new insights into cancer, heart disease and the genetic controls governing cellular protein release.
summary: UCLA-developed nanovials that cap and trap cells and their secretions act like test tubes on the cellular scale. These nanovials have helped reveal new insights into cancer, heart disease and the genetic levers that drive cells to release proteins.
author: Phys.org

title: Cornell engineers examine how nanoparticles form eye‑catching patterns
content: Cornell engineers are researching the mechanisms that cause nanoparticles to self‑assemble into striking patterns, drawing analogies to the stripes of tigers and zebras and to quantum‑dot arrangements. Their work focuses on identifying the factors that drive the formation of these eye‑catching structures.
summary: A group of Cornell engineers is investigating what drives the formation of eye‑catching patterns in nanoparticles. Their research draws parallels to the stripes of tigers and zebras and the arrangement of quantum dots.
author: Phys.org

title: Japanese researchers find upside-down atom-thin layers can direct heat in stacked chips
content: Stacking chips vertically can boost computer speed, but the arrangement generates a heating challenge. Researchers in Japan report that turning atom‑thin layers upside down can direct heat toward desired pathways, offering a simple method to manage thermal flow in stacked chip architectures.
summary: Stacking chips on top of one another could keep computers getting faster, but it creates a heating problem. Researchers from Japan have found that flipping atom‑thin layers upside down can steer that heat where it needs to go.
author: Phys.org

title: Bubble of absolute nothing could trigger sudden end of universe, columnist says
content: Columnist Leah Crane writes about the theoretical possibility of a “bubble of absolutely nothing” – a region of truly empty space – existing somewhere in the cosmos. She discusses how such a void could arise and the potential danger it might pose if it were to affect our universe.
summary: A bubble of absolutely nothing, described as truly empty space, could exist somewhere in the cosmos. Leah Crane writes that such a bubble could cause the universe to end suddenly.
author: New Scientist

title: 2096 Future Report: Humans Talk to Whales, Cure Alzheimer’s, Build Mars Base
content: A special report set in 2096 describes a world where humans can communicate with sperm whales, have largely eliminated Alzheimer’s disease, and where synthetic beings are constructing a base on Mars. The piece also poses the question of whether non‑human species will ever forgive humanity for the environmental damage it has caused.
summary: In 2096, humans can communicate with sperm whales, have mostly eradicated Alzheimer’s disease, and synthetic beings are developing a base on Mars. The report questions whether non‑human species will ever forgive humanity for the damage inflicted on Earth.
author: New Scientist

title: Nuclear explosion in space could disable 98% of satellites within a week, experts warn
content: Experts warn that a single nuclear explosion in space would have global, long‑lasting repercussions, disabling almost every satellite and creating technological chaos. They estimate the blast could disable about 98 percent of satellites within a week, with recovery taking years.
summary: Nuclear explosion in space could disable 98% of satellites within a week, experts warn.
author: New Scientist

title: New Scientist writer uses evidence and imagination to craft 2096 future scenario
content:
The author of a New Scientist feature on the magazine’s 70th anniversary explains how they crafted a speculative portrait of the world in 2096. Describing themselves as a lifelong science‑fiction enthusiast, they began by gathering ideas from colleagues at the magazine and then tried to shape those varied concepts into a coherent narrative, noting that different imagined futures often contradict one another.

To anchor the story in real science, the writer turned to climate‑change projections, which they say are based on atmospheric physics that can be modelled, though the ultimate outcome depends on human political choices. Population trends also informed the piece, with the author highlighting the possibility that the end of the century could be the first time global populations begin to decline. These strands provided a factual backdrop for the imagined future.

The author found AI especially difficult to predict, noting that their own views on the technology have shifted since the release of ChatGPT in 2022. To avoid letting AI dominate the narrative, they limited its role to a “boring middle option” and invented an AI‑fuelled financial crisis that would lead to regulatory limits on the technology. The piece also introduces an International Treaty on Non‑Human Personhood, inspired by contemporary shifts in attitudes toward animals and artificial intelligence, and explores how such legal recognition could affect the world.

Interviews with dozens of experts revealed limited interdisciplinary forecasting, especially regarding how climate change might intersect with public‑health trends and how AI could influence various scientific fields. The author reflects that, while they and many interviewees are unlikely to live to see 2096, a seven‑decade horizon offers a useful distance for speculation, allowing imagination to fill the gaps that evidence alone cannot close.
summary: The author wrote a New Scientist feature for its 70th anniversary that imagines life in the year 2096, grounding the narrative in climate‑change forecasts, population trends and a limited AI scenario. The piece also proposes an International Treaty on Non‑Human Personhood and draws on interviews with dozens of experts.
author: New Scientist

title: Study finds coupled Antarctic sea‑ice expansion and glacial circulation lower CO₂
content:
Ocean carbon sequestration under glacial conditions: insights from a new MIT‑UQAR study

A recent paper in Science Advances investigates how processes in the Southern Ocean during glacial periods influence global ocean carbon storage and atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂) drawdown. The research, conducted by scientists from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the Université du Québec à Rimouski, examines the combined effects of ocean cooling, sea‑ice expansion, and altered circulation rather than treating each factor in isolation.

The authors explain that the ocean contributes to the carbon cycle through three main mechanisms. Solubility allows colder, denser water to dissolve more CO₂ and sink into the deep ocean. Biological activity transfers CO₂ to surface phytoplankton, whose organic matter eventually sinks and is remineralized. Disequilibrium reflects the difference between the amount of carbon water could hold in long‑term balance with the atmosphere and the amount actually present, shaped by biology, circulation and gas exchange.

Model experiments that altered Antarctic sea ice or glacial circulation alone produced only slight increases in atmospheric CO₂, suggesting limited impact on carbon storage when each process is considered separately. However, a “full” experiment that combined extensive sea ice, glacial circulation and cooler temperatures yielded a clear decline in atmospheric CO₂, indicating greater ocean carbon uptake. The increase in stored carbon was dominated not by solubility but by the disequilibrium pool, which the authors attribute to reduced exposure of upwelled deep‑water carbon to the atmosphere when sea ice and circulation act together.

Coupling sea‑ice expansion with altered circulation amplified the CO₂ drawdown, because the combined effect shortens the time surface waters spend in contact with the atmosphere, sending more upwelled carbon back into the ocean interior. The study also explored implications for the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC). Model scenarios in which the AMOC slowed caused the boundary between Southern Ocean and North Atlantic waters to become shallower, limiting deep‑water mixing and slowing carbon release to the atmosphere. The authors note that a potential AMOC collapse could either further isolate Southern Ocean carbon or, if accompanied by warming and reduced Antarctic sea ice, increase carbon loss.

The paper lists Jonathan Lauderdale of MIT’s Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences and the Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy as a lead author, alongside Raffaele Ferrari, Sandy Grégorio and Louis‑Philippe Nadeau. Funding sources include the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada, the Canada First Research Excellence Fund, Schmidt Sciences LLC, the MIT Climate Grand Challenge, the Simons Collaboration on Computational BIOgeochemical Modeling of marine EcosystemS, and the U.S. National Science Foundation.
summary: Study finds coupled Antarctic sea‑ice expansion and glacial circulation lower CO₂.

title: MIT scientists find pink noise boosts brain's nighttime cleaning waves
content: MIT researchers found that delivering carefully timed bursts of gentle pink noise while a person sleeps can amplify the brain’s natural cleaning waves that remove potentially harmful waste. The discovery suggests a possible route to treatments that enhance sleep and memory and may lessen the accumulation of proteins associated with Alzheimer’s disease.
summary: MIT scientists discovered that carefully timed bursts of gentle pink noise during sleep can strengthen the brain’s natural cleaning waves that flush away potentially harmful waste. The finding may lead to new treatments to improve sleep and memory and possibly reduce protein buildup linked to Alzheimer’s disease.
author: Science Daily

title: Study finds sex, genetics, menopause affect Alzheimer’s risk and chronic pain
content: New research indicates that biological sex, genetics, and menopause can dramatically affect Alzheimer’s risk, treatment responses, and chronic pain conditions such as fibromyalgia. The study also found surprising differences in immune activity and gut‑brain interactions, suggesting potential for more personalized treatments for neurological disorders.
summary: New research shows that biological sex, genetics and menopause can strongly influence Alzheimer’s risk, treatment responses, and chronic pain conditions such as fibromyalgia. The study also identified differences in immune activity and gut‑brain interactions, suggesting potential for more personalized neurological disorder treatments.
author: Science Daily

title: NASA offers $1 million Moon Base Challenge to U. S. Students
content:
NASA is offering $1 million in its new Moon Base Challenge, inviting U.S. students to develop innovative solutions for building humanity’s first permanent lunar outpost.  

Ideas ranging from power systems to astronaut safety could help make long‑term life on the Moon possible and pave the way to Mars.
summary: NASA is offering $1 million in its new Moon Base Challenge, inviting U. S.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists create strong insulation from emergency blankets for lunar habitats
content:
Scientists turned thin plastic used in emergency blankets into strong insulation that could help astronauts survive extreme temperatures.  

Built from hundreds of stacked layers, the material withstands crushing pressure without losing its thermal protection, potentially paving the way for tougher, longer‑lasting lunar habitats.
summary: Scientists have turned the thin plastic used in emergency blankets into a remarkably strong insulation that could help astronauts survive the Moon's extreme temperatures. The material, built from hundreds of stacked layers, withstands crushing pressure without losing its thermal protection, potentially enabling tougher, longer‑lasting lunar habitats.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists find heart ages unevenly, with inflammation in valves and vessels
content: Scientists have found that the heart ages unevenly, with inflammation and scarring concentrated in the valves and major blood vessels rather than the heart muscle. The discovery challenges long‑standing assumptions about cardiac aging and may guide researchers in developing new ways to protect the heart as we grow older.
summary: Scientists discovered that the heart ages unevenly, with inflammation and scarring concentrated in the valves and major blood vessels rather than the heart muscle. The findings challenge long‑standing assumptions about cardiac aging and may guide new ways to protect the heart as people grow older.
author: Science Daily

title: Vitamin B12 reverses developmental defects in worms with Verheij syndrome mutation
content:
Scientists discovered vitamin B12 largely reversed developmental abnormalities in worms carrying a mutation linked to Verheij syndrome, a rare disorder that causes growth problems and developmental delays.  

Similar metabolic changes were identified in human patients, suggesting that vitamin B12 could inspire new treatments for rare genetic diseases.
summary: Scientists found that vitamin B12 largely reversed developmental abnormalities in worms carrying a genetic mutation linked to Verheij syndrome. Similar metabolic changes were observed in human patients, suggesting the vitamin could inform new treatments for rare genetic diseases.
author: Science Daily

title: Wearable ultrasound patch speeds REM sleep entry, extends duration without drugs
content:
A wearable ultrasound patch created by researchers at the University of Texas is reported to increase restorative sleep without the need for medication or surgery. The device delivers gentle ultrasound to deep brain regions, which the study found helped participants reach REM sleep 43 minutes faster and stay in that stage 16 minutes longer on average.

In addition to the sleep benefits, the technology showed promising effects on stress regulation and on brain circuits linked to emotion, according to the researchers’ findings.
summary: University of Texas researchers developed a wearable ultrasound patch that gently stimulates deep brain regions to promote REM sleep. In trials, participants entered REM sleep 43 minutes faster, stayed 16 minutes longer, and showed promising effects on stress regulation and emotion‑related brain circuits.
author: Science Daily

title: European Hera spacecraft images cratered side of asteroid Didymos after NASA impact
content:
European spacecraft Hera has revealed a mysterious, crater‑covered side of the asteroid Didymos. The discovery comes as the mission prepares to investigate the aftermath of NASA’s historic 2022 asteroid impact.  

The data could uncover new clues about the collision and help turn asteroid deflection into a powerful defense against future threats to Earth.
summary: A European spacecraft has revealed a mysterious, crater-covered side of the asteroid Didymos. The mission is preparing to investigate the aftermath of NASA’s historic 2022 asteroid impact.
author: Science Daily

title: HIV researcher Jade Pagkas-Bather says Trump officials interfered with NIH grant
content: Researchers forced to scrap original studies as NIH rethinks grants not in ‘alignment’ with administration’s priorities Dr Jade Pagkas-Bather received her first grant from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) in June 2025 – a milestone in any researcher’s career. She planned to study basic income as a medical intervention: her randomized control trial would test whether monthly grants of $500-cash helped poor, HIV-positive young people in Chicago stick with treatment. Her hypothesis was as straightforward as it was cutting.
summary: Dr Jade Pagkas-Bather received her first NIH grant in June 2025 to test monthly $500 cash payments for poor HIV‑positive young people in Chicago. She says NIH forced her to scrap the original study because the grant was not aligned with the Trump administration’s priorities.
author: Guardian Science

title: NASA Welcomes Jim Mirandy as Civil Servant Quality Assurance Specialist
content: 3 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) Jim Mirandy, quality assurance specialist at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, poses for a photograph at the High Pressure Gas Facility on Nov. 10, 2026. Mirandy is now a NASA civil servant at Stennis as part of the administrator’s directive to strengthen technical core competencies within the civil service workforce. NASA/Danny Nowlin The rumble of a rocket engine might be considered a soundtrack for Jim Mirandy’s life. Mirandy has grown up with NASA as a constant presence, and his path to becoming a civil servant at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, has been decades in the making. Hired under the agency’s workforce directive to restore core competencies by converting contractors to civil service, Mirandy is now a quality assurance specialist after 30 years of working as a contractor supporting NASA. “Discovery is an important job, and it is exciting to be a part of that process,” said Mirandy. “As a nation, we lead the world in space exploration, and we make that dream of reaching for the stars a reality.” His work at the nation’s largest rocket propulsion test site directly supports the agency’s mission to return American astronauts to the Moon through the Artemis program and ensure American leadership in space. By retaining Mirandy’s facility-specific expertise as a civil servant, NASA ensures that the critical propulsion testing at NASA Stennis continues to be executed with safety and quality in mind. Mirandy describes his team as an integral part of the process that provides a second set of eyes with a focus on potential hazards. As a quality assurance specialist, he serves as the agency’s close call investigator at the center, helps lead the Voluntary Protection Program, and participates in the Striving to Achieve Real Safety committee, an employee safety committee that works to keep the site safe. Mirandy also has a long resume of critical institutional contributions, including creating high pressure and cryogenic training classes that he taught for 10 years, and helping establish safety protocols throughout various locations at the center. Mirandy’s connection to America’s space agency began in childhood living in Titusville, Florida. His father, Wes Mirandy, worked for Rocketdyne at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, and Mirandy’s nearby elementary school regularly gathered to watch launches. Later, his father worked as the A-1 test stand manager for space shuttle main engine testing at NASA Stennis. “My father was by far my greatest mentor,” said Mirandy. “My dad always included us whenever he worked on something around the house, so we picked up a knack for examining problems and fixing things. When I arrived at Stennis Space Center, many of his friends and coworkers took the time to help me succeed at my job. They took the time to explain the test stands and other systems and how they worked.” A knack for fixing things helped launch Mirandy’s career at Michoud Assembly Facility in New Orleans. He started working hands-on as a mechanic on the Space Shuttle External Tank. When an unexpected incident occurred in a production cell, Mirandy stepped up to help the operations and safety team resolve the issue. This moment shifted his career trajectory into safety and quality. Mirandy found his way to NASA Stennis and brought an understanding of systems and operations with him. A resident of Bay St. Louis and a graduate of the University of Southern Mississippi, Mirandy is motivated by helping people, keeping them safe, and improving processes. “Your reward for working safely today is tomorrow,” said Mirandy. title: NASA Receives 16th Consecutive Clean Financial Audit Opinion
content:
NASA has received an unmodified, or “clean,” opinion from an external auditor on its fiscal year 2026 financial statements, marking the 16th consecutive year the agency has achieved this rating. This opinion is the highest possible audit result, certifying that NASA’s financial statements accurately present the agency’s financial position and conform with Generally Accepted Accounting Principles for federal agencies.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman stated that the agency’s responsibility is to be disciplined stewards of resources entrusted by the American people while delivering on expected missions. He noted that the 16th consecutive clean audit reflects a long record of financial accountability, which NASA intends to pair with the urgency and execution required for upcoming missions. The 2026 Agency Financial Report, which demonstrates the agency’s commitment to transparency, also spotlights advancements in NASA missions, objectives, and workforce development.

The report highlights several key achievements during fiscal year 2026. NASA’s 10-day Artemis II mission successfully completed a test flight around the Moon with four crew members, setting a record for the distance astronauts have traveled from Earth. Additionally, the agency launched the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope ahead of schedule to study dark matter, dark energy, and exoplanets. The experimental X-59 quiet supersonic aircraft also achieved a major milestone by flying faster than the speed of sound for the first time.

Beyond these scientific and engineering milestones, NASA announced transformative agencywide initiatives, including plans to build a Moon Base near the lunar South Pole. The agency also launched NASA Force with the U.S. Office of Personnel Management to recruit top engineers and technologists, announced an agencywide realignment to increase mission focus, and welcomed additional signatories to the Artemis Accords.
summary: NASA received an unmodified opinion from an external auditor on its fiscal year 2026 financial statements, marking the 16th consecutive year of this top rating. The agency’s report highlights financial accountability alongside mission achievements, including the Artemis II test flight and the launch of the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.

title: Perseverance rover finds hydrated silica rocks in Idubi area of Mars
content:
NASA’s Perseverance rover has returned new observations from the “Idubi” area, a section of ancient Martian crust located in the Lac de Charmes region outside Jezero crater. On Sol 2023 (Oct. 29, 2026) the rover’s left Mastcam‑Z camera captured a bright, silica‑rich rock at a local mean solar time of 13:03:53. The same Sol, at 17:33:55 LMST, the SHERLOC WATSON camera on the rover’s turret recorded a close‑up view of a similar light‑toned rock.

Analysis of data from the rover’s SuperCam instrument confirms that the light‑toned fragments are not igneous but are rich in hydrated silica. Hydrated silica can form in a variety of aqueous settings on Earth, including hydrothermal, pedogenic and groundwater environments, making such deposits valuable for reconstructing Mars’ hydrological history.

The Perseverance team notes that hydrated silica is of particular astrobiological interest because of its capacity to preserve microfossils. Earlier encounters with silica‑rich rocks on the inner rim of Jezero crater yielded deposits that were too small for proximity science instruments to acquire high‑resolution chemical and mineralogical data. By contrast, the Idubi rocks are large enough to support a detailed proximity‑science campaign, which is now underway.

The update was written by Candice Bedford, a research scientist at Purdue University, and posted on Nov. 16, 2026. It is part of the ongoing Perseverance mission updates that document the rover’s scientific investigations and findings.
summary: NASA's Perseverance rover photographed bright, silica‑rich rocks in the Idubi area of the Lac de Charmes region outside Jezero crater on Oct. 29 2026 (Sol 2023). SuperCam data confirmed the light‑toned rocks are hydrated silica, and a proximity science campaign is now investigating them for clues to Mars’ water history and potential biosignature preservation.

title: Axonnic launches forearm EMG sleeve that decodes finger movement and estimates force
content: Hi HN! We’re Arsh and Max, founders of Axonnic ( https://axonnic. Com ). We’ve developed a forearm sleeve that reads muscle activity to decode finger movements and estimate fingertip force, while leaving the hands bare. It’s used to record human movement and generate training data for dextrous robots. Here’s a demo video: https://youtube. Com/shorts/xBrocTc9cfA We’ve found that electromyography (EMG) is a much better way to train robots than by video alone because video only captures movement, not muscle activity or the effort behind the movement. A useful signal can be present even when the hand barely moves; just maintaining a grip involves muscle activation. The subtle muscle movements that can barely be picked up in video are the most important details for activities like sewing and delicate assembly. The sleeve has 64 channels of surface electromyography, or EMG. Electrodes on the skin detect electrical activity from muscles in the forearm. We distribute sensors across the forearm so as to not overfit to one muscle group. We synchronize EMG with hand tracking to train a model that predicts finger joint angles, then we run the decoder solely from EMG, adding in fingertip force estimates that have been calibrated from finger presses on force sensors. When the user takes the sleeve off then puts it back on again, the electrode positions change, so we run tests over separate wearings. In one case, we ran a 215-second recording, four days after training, without any recalibration, and compared the results with Apple Vision Pro hand tracking. The result was just 6.9° error across 20 joint angles. We’ve published the measurements and evaluation details here: https://axonnic. Com/benchmarks. We faced many challenges doing recordings in factories, including wireless interference and unreliable off-the-shelf hardware. This led to some bad recordings and the need to repeat data collection. For that reason, we’re developing our own electronics that use a wired PCB design that will eliminate interference and timing inconsistencies. Axonnic grew out of Max's EMG research at Oxford. We looked at using the technology for computer control, then we thought a more promising use-case was in capturing the effort involved in skilled manual tasks. This technology could be described as a computer to human interface. Where computers gain insight and learn from human skills. Sewing particularly stood out because the material deforms and the operator is constantly adjusting grip and tension. Maxim has an Oxford MBiol and conducted research on high-density surface EMG. He previously built internal tools at Skyscanner and worked at Voxblock across PCB development and supply chain. Arsh studied medicine at Oxford and has research experience applying machine learning to medical imaging, alongside software and robotics projects. Together we have built the sleeve, decoding software and data-collection system and tested them in industrial settings. So far we have the tech being used to record sewing and other manual tasks at a European manufacturer, which signed an LOI for support with robotic implementation. We have also collected construction demonstrations involving electricians, plumbers and demolition work. These are pilot and data-collection examples. Separately, our public demos include controlling a Proception robotic hand from forearm EMG. If you’ve done any of your own trials for training robots for manual tasks, we’d love to hear about what tasks you were trying to train for and how the trials went. We’re happy to discuss the hardware, calibration and models here in the comments. Thanks! Https://axonnic. Com Comments URL: https://news. Ycombinator. Com/item? Id=50522776 Points: 25 # Comments: 10

title: Supreme Court declines appeal, leaves injunction blocking DEI grant cancellations in place
content:

The Court’s order keeps the injunction in place, preventing the government from rescinding the grants in question.

The injunction applies to seven researchers in California. A federal district judge had found that the government’s actions violated the First Amendment, a finding that could have broader implications beyond the seven cases. The Supreme Court issued no written opinion and no justice filed a dissent.

The lawsuit was brought by a large group of researchers from the University of California, Berkeley and UC San Francisco. They challenged the termination of grants originally issued by several federal agencies, including the National Institutes of Health and the Department of Transportation. The grants were canceled because the agencies determined they violated a Trump executive order that barred the use of DEI. The government had not defined DEI, and the targeted grants were identified largely through keyword searches.

content:
The rapid expansion of large‑language‑model development has spurred a sudden rush to build hyperscale data centers.  This surge has outpaced any coordinated effort to plan how the required electricity will be supplied cleanly or to assess the impact on ratepayers.  Consequently, even basic information about what is being constructed has been hard to obtain.

A new study has quantified the energy use and estimated emissions of hyperscale facilities operating in the United States from May 2024 to April 2025.  While the analysis could not separate AI‑specific compute from more traditional data‑service workloads, it establishes a clear baseline that can be tracked in the future.  The study notes that these centers consume about 2 % of U.S. electricity.

The research team began with a commercial database listing 675 facilities identified through news reports, company statements, and satellite imagery.  Facilities lacking a reported electrical capacity or verifiable large‑building infrastructure were excluded, leaving 403 data centers.  Those remaining have an average electrical capacity of roughly 40 megawatts.
summary: A study of hyperscale data centers operating in the United States between May 2024 and April 2025 found they use about 2% of the country’s electricity. Researchers identified 403 verified facilities with an average electrical capacity of roughly 40 megawatts after narrowing a starting list of 675 sites.

title: Three small failures combined to take down Microsoft 365
content:

A preliminary Post‑Incident Report (PIR) explains that the latent bug, changes in traffic patterns, and reduced server capacity together knocked much of the Microsoft 365 and Exchange infrastructure offline.

The outage began on November 12 at 16:20 UTC and ended on November 13 at 16:10 UTC, lasting just under 24 hours.  Microsoft kept additional monitoring in place until November 14.  The disruption quickly spread to businesses and public offices that rely on Microsoft’s cloud and email exchange services.

The incident is identified in Microsoft’s logs as EX1550543 and MO1550821.  Full details are available only to Microsoft 365 administrators, but Office Watch has reproduced the preliminary report, and the University of Pennsylvania maintains an archive of Microsoft’s service‑health updates.  Microsoft’s final status for the event is “a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents.”
summary: Three small failures combined to take down Microsoft 365.

title: Grand Theft Auto’s radio stations drive music culture
content: Featuring hundreds of songs from the hippest real-world artists, the radio stations in Rockstar’s crime sagas are as hotly anticipated as the storylines. Gradually, the asphalt gives way to rural backwaters, and so the sounds of Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas’s local radio also change: less gangster rap and more twangin’ country – the grizzled croon of Merle Haggard and yearning warble of Patsy Cline. The Grand Theft Auto games are massive, stretching across many, many square miles of virtual terrain. Their soundtracks, relayed mostly via in-game radio stations, are manifold. And these two aspects, plus the personal experiences each player brings to the game, mean everyone has a different favourite musical memory from the smash-hit crime series. For acclaimed electronic musician Flying Lotus, it is all the hours he spent cavorting around 2004’s San Andreas that remain special. “It felt like the first time a game saw a different side of culture – black culture,” he says over the phone. “It felt like we were being seen. And with the extent of the music, all the cool California hip-hop, it felt like someone actually cared.”
summary: The Grand Theft Auto series includes radio stations that feature hundreds of songs from real‑world artists and are eagerly anticipated by players. Contributors such as Flying Lotus, Wavves and Nite Jewel discuss the curation and cultural impact of the game’s soundtracks.

title: EF1 tornado touches down in Delaware's Salem Woods, second November tornado since 1950
content:
The National Weather Service confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down southeast of Newark in the Salem Woods neighbourhood of Delaware on Thursday. The funnel measured about 160 metres in width, traveled a path of 4.4 miles (7.1 km) and produced estimated peak winds of up to 100 mph (161 km/h). No injuries or fatalities were reported, but the storm damaged windows and roofs on several homes, caused a large hotel sign to fall onto parked cars, and overturned a semi‑truck on I‑95.

According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, this is only the second recorded November tornado in Delaware since 1950, the first occurring in 1989. The same weather system that produced the Delaware tornado also generated severe thunderstorms in Argentina’s central Córdoba province, delivering hailstones the size of baseballs and up to 73 mm of rain in six hours. Such storms are typical for the region during this season.
summary: EF1 tornado touches down in Delaware's Salem Woods, second November tornado since 1950.

content: Maryland Governor Wes Moore (D) said on Sunday that he is still weighing a 2028 presidential run. In an interview on Noosphere with independent journalist Chuck Todd, Moore explained that he is “still sorting” out the decision to move from the governor’s mansion to the White House.

content: Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday blasted “incoming freshmen” Democrats elected following the 2026 midterm elections for “acting like prosecutors” in joining lawmakers’ calls to open investigations into President Trump and his administration. Fox News host Mark Levin asked Blanche on his show “Life, Liberty & Levin” if Congress can act “like a judiciary and…

title: Wadden Sea faces danger list threat from extraction, tourism, and fishing
content:
The Wadden Sea, a vast intertidal system spanning the coasts of the Netherlands, Germany, and Denmark, faces potential inclusion on the UNESCO World Heritage in Danger list. This unique habitat, recognized as the largest unbroken system of intertidal sand and mud flats globally, was granted World Heritage status in 2009. The area is characterized by a dramatic transformation in its landscape, shifting from unbroken water with offshore sandy islands at high tide to a complex maze of deep channels, drying sandbanks, salt marshes, and mud flats a few hours later.

Despite its ecological significance and rich marine life, the Wadden Sea is under pressure from various human activities. Extraction industries, tourism, and fishing are cited as factors taking a toll on the environment. These pressures threaten the integrity of the habitat that supports a wealth of biodiversity, prompting concerns about its current status and future conservation efforts within the World Heritage framework.
summary: The Wadden Sea, a transboundary intertidal system spanning the Netherlands, Germany, and Denmark, was awarded UNESCO World Heritage status in 2009. Extraction industries, tourism, and fishing are currently taking a toll on the region's marine life and bird populations.
author: Guardian Environment

title: UK EV target cuts would hurt car industry, ministers warned
content:
Experts have warned that weakening the United Kingdom’s zero‑emissions vehicle (ZEV) mandate would slow the electric‑vehicle market and hinder efforts to reduce the cost of living. They argue that such moves would hurt the car industry, consumers, campaigners and the broader economy.  

The Climate Change Committee (CCC) is scheduled to write to ministers on Wednesday, outlining how changes to the ZEV mandate could affect the cost of living and the country’s net‑zero targets.
summary: Campaigners and experts warn that weakening the UK's zero emissions vehicle mandate would slow the market and harm consumers. The climate change committee is set to write to ministers about the impact of these changes on the cost of living and net zero targets.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Huge waves up to 50ft force pier closures on California coast
content:
Large waves up to 50 feet flooded southern California streets and prompted evacuation warnings near coastal cities. The California coast was pummeled on Sunday by these huge waves, which inundated beaches, flooded local streets, and forced the closure of popular piers.

Additionally, the National Weather Service office for the San Francisco Bay Area warned that surf up to 35 feet (11 meters) was possible, along with dangerous rip currents and sneaker waves.
summary: Large waves up to 50ft flooded southern California streets and prompted an evacuation warning near a coastal city, forcing the closure of popular piers. The National Weather Service office for the San Francisco Bay Area warned that surf up to 35ft was possible, along with dangerous rip currents and sneaker waves.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Preliminary study finds clue for diagnosing CTE in living patients
content: Scientists have identified a potential diagnostic marker for chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE). The study indicates that measuring a toxic protein linked to Alzheimer’s disease may eventually aid in diagnosing CTE in individuals who have sustained repeated head injuries, such as football players.
summary: Scientists found a hint that measuring a toxic protein tied to Alzheimer's disease might help diagnose a different brain disease. The finding could aid diagnosis in football players and others who have suffered repeated blows to the head.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Ice Baths: Popular Recovery Method for Athletes and Gym-Goers
content: Ice baths have become one of the most popular recovery strategies in sport. They are used by elite athletes and recreational gym‑goers to reduce soreness and recuperate more quickly after exercising.
summary: Ice baths have become a popular recovery strategy in sport. They are used by elite athletes and recreational gym-goers to reduce soreness and recover more quickly after exercising.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Standardized Markers Let Labs Reliably Isolate Thymic Epithelial Cells
content: Standardized markers and extraction methods now allow laboratories to reliably isolate thymic epithelial cells (TECs). These “teacher” cells, which instruct immune T cells to attack foreign invaders while preventing attacks on healthy tissues, comprise less than 1 % of all cells in the thymus gland. Because TECs are so rare, research groups have spent decades struggling to agree on how to properly study them. The new protocols provide a consistent approach, enabling more accurate and reproducible investigations of this critical component of the immune system.
summary: The thymus gland uses rare “teacher” cells, thymic epithelial cells (TECs), to train immune T cells to attack foreign invaders and prevent autoimmunity. Researchers have spent decades struggling to isolate TECs, which make up less than 1% of all cells in the gland.
author: Medical Xpress

title: National poll: Parents say pets boost kids' emotional health but expect them to care
content: A national poll found that most parents say pets benefit children’s emotional health, yet they still expect kids to help with care. Parents note that when a new pet arrives as a holiday or birthday surprise, children often do not follow through on the pet‑care responsibilities they anticipate.
summary: Most parents say pets benefit children's emotional health. Parents expect kids to help with care, but kids may not always follow through on the pet‑care responsibilities.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Inpatient Alcohol Treatment Group Attendance Drops, Racial Gaps Persist
content:
A recent study published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs found a steep decline in the use of mutual‑help groups among people in inpatient alcohol treatment.  The proportion of patients who attended Alcoholics Anonymous or a similar group at least once a week fell from more than half of the sample to fewer than four in ten over a seven‑year period.

The research also highlighted significant racial and ethnic disparities.  Latinx/Hispanic, Black, and American Indian/Alaska Native patients were less likely than white patients to attend weekly, even after the analysis adjusted for factors such as age, employment status, and alcohol use.
summary: Inpatient Alcohol Treatment Group Attendance Drops, Racial Gaps Persist.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Cannabis use disorder linked to higher odds of suicidal thoughts
content: Cannabis use is increasingly common and socially accepted, yet health risks exist, particularly with problematic use. A new study published by Rutgers University in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs found that adults with cannabis use disorder have significantly higher odds of suicidal ideation.
summary: A new study in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs found that adults with cannabis use disorder have significantly higher odds of suicidal ideation. The research was published by Rutgers University.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Archaeologists explore wealth inequality among Europe's early herders
content: Archaeologists are investigating the level of inequality in prehistoric societies, focusing on Europe’s early herders. They aim to determine how wealth and status can be measured in cultures that left no written records, tax registers, or census data.
summary: Archaeologists examine how unequal prehistoric European herding societies were. They consider ways to measure wealth in cultures lacking written records, tax registers or census data.
author: Phys.org

title: Lake Baikal, the world’s largest freshwater lake, shows signs of recovery
content:
Lake Baikal in Siberia, which contains roughly 20 % of the world’s surface freshwater, is described as the most voluminous freshwater lake and is now reported to be recovering after decades of decline. The lake was designated a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1996 because of its significant biodiversity.  

Over the past century Baikal experienced considerable decline, a trend linked to aridification spreading across East Asia, even as Lake Superior remains the largest freshwater lake by surface area. The recent recovery marks a reversal of that long‑term downturn.
summary: Lake Baikal in Siberia holds about 20% of the world’s surface freshwater, making it the most voluminous freshwater lake. After a century of decline linked to aridification across East Asia, the lake is now recovering.
author: Phys.org

title: Ancient 3.95‑billion‑year‑old rocks found in northern China illuminate early crust formation
content:
Earth is estimated to be about 4.5 billion years old, but rocks from its earliest era are exceedingly scarce. Researchers have identified a set of rocks in northern China that date to roughly 3.95 billion years ago, placing them among the oldest known specimens on the planet.

The newly discovered rocks are attracting attention because they provide fresh evidence about the processes that formed and altered Earth’s crust during its formative period.
summary: Rocks dating about 3.95 billion years were discovered in northern China, making them among the oldest known on Earth. They are revealing new clues about how Earth's crust formed and evolved.
author: Phys.org

title: Lens may let astronomers see supernova SN Ares two more times in ~70 years
content:
Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope identified an exploding star, designated SN Ares, whose light was magnified and split by the gravitational lensing of a massive galaxy cluster. The detection corresponds to a universe age of 4.9 billion years.  

A paper describing the find was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Oct. 23, and it includes a prediction for when the remaining distorted images of SN Ares are expected to arrive, suggesting the cosmic lens could reveal the same supernova two additional times over roughly a 70‑year span.
summary: Thanks to the gravitational lensing caused by a massive galaxy cluster and high-resolution images from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), astronomers discovered an exploding star when the universe was 4.9 billion years old. content: An eye‑tracking study conducted in Sudan investigated whether culture shapes how people view art. Separately, Old Dongola, situated on the banks of the Nile in northern Sudan, is now an abandoned settlement that looked very different hundreds of years ago.
summary: An eye‑tracking study was carried out in Sudan to examine whether culture shapes how people look at art. The research was set at Old Dongola, an abandoned settlement on the banks of the Nile in northern Sudan that looked very different hundreds of years ago.

title: White dwarf flashes radio waves every 8 minutes, paired with sun‑like red dwarf
content:
Since 2022, astronomers have been puzzled by a new class of objects known as long‑period radio transients. These sources emit bright flashes of radio waves into space at intervals ranging from a few minutes to a few hours.  

Some of these transients have been traced back to binary systems that consist of a small, dim, cool red dwarf and a white dwarf, a stellar remnant.
summary: A white dwarf is flashing bright radio waves about every eight minutes. It is in a binary system with a red dwarf that looks a lot like the Sun.

content: The article notes that, from a naked‑eye perspective, stars appear stable and predictable, with the Sun described as a low‑mass star expected to shine steadily for billions of years. title: Four-month rehab after ACL surgery may protect young adults from early knee osteoarthritis
content:
A new study indicates that a specific exercise regimen may protect young adults from early knee osteoarthritis after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) surgery. Researchers observed that participants who completed a four‑month supervised rehabilitation program experienced improvements in pain, muscle strength and quality of life, while the program did not damage knee cartilage.

The results counter concerns that exercise could exacerbate injured knees and suggest the protocol could influence future recovery approaches for patients undergoing ACL reconstruction.
summary: Researchers found that a four-month supervised rehabilitation program improved pain, muscle strength and quality of life after ACL surgery without damaging knee cartilage. The study suggests the exercise may protect young adults from early knee osteoarthritis and challenges fears that exercise worsens injured knees.

content: Scientists have developed an efficient method that converts used coffee grounds into a potential source of biodiesel while preserving the remaining material for other renewable fuels and valuable chemicals. The discovery suggests that millions of tons of discarded coffee waste could become a useful resource for sustainable energy.
summary: Scientists have created an efficient process that turns used coffee grounds into a potential source of biodiesel. The method also preserves leftover material for other renewable fuels and valuable chemicals, potentially converting millions of tons of coffee waste into sustainable energy.
author: Science Daily

title: Leonid meteor shower peaks this week, bright display expected 17‑18 November
content: The Leonid meteor shower, an annual display that appears to radiate from the constellation Leo in the eastern sky as Earth moves through a comet’s debris stream, is set to reach its peak this week. Observers are advised that the shower’s most active period will occur during the night of 17–18 November. Under ideal viewing conditions, up to 10–15 meteors per hour may be seen, offering a brief but bright spectacle despite modest overall numbers.
summary: The annual Leonid meteor shower reaches its peak this week, with the most active period on the night of 17–18 November. Under ideal conditions observers may see 10–15 meteors per hour, noted for their brilliance.

title: Puncak Jaya Glaciers Shrink to Tiny Fragments, Near Disappearance
content:
The Indonesian Sudirman Range on the island of New Guinea contains one of the world’s few tropical glaciers.  NASA Earth Observatory’s latest images show the dramatic retreat of the ice that once capped the highest peaks of the range, including the summit of Puncak Jaya.  A false‑color image taken in 1988 by the Landsat 5 Thematic Mapper (TM) and a newer image from 2026 acquired by the Landsat 9 Operational Land Imager (OLI) are placed side by side.  In the older picture, blue‑shaded ice covers several ridges, while brown shows exposed rock and green indicates lower‑elevation vegetation.  The 2026 image reveals only small blue fragments of ice; the majority of the former glacial area is now bare brown rock.

In 1988 the glaciers on Puncak Jaya spanned roughly 4.31 square kilometers (1.66 square miles).  By September 2025 satellite and aerial data indicated that the ice had shrunk to about 0.09 square kilometers (0.03 square miles) – a loss of roughly 98 percent of the original extent.  The remaining ice is limited to a dozen soccer‑field‑sized patches.  An aerial survey scheduled for December 2026 is expected to provide a more precise estimate of the ice that remains in that year.

Thickness measurements at the primary monitoring site on the East Northwall Firn show a dramatic decline.  The ice was 32 meters (105 feet) thick in 2010, fell to 4 meters (13 feet) in 2023, and by November 2024 the ice at that location had disappeared entirely.  As the glaciers thin, they fragment, creating more exposed edges that accelerate melt.  The 2026 image shows freshly uncovered bedrock between the remaining ice remnants, and although snow still falls, it does not accumulate enough to rebuild the ice.

A glacier must be thick enough to flow downhill under its own weight and must receive more snowfall than melt.  The remaining ice at Puncak Jaya has thinned so far that it no longer flows; it exists only as stagnant patches.  “While small ice remnants persist in high‑altitude crevices around Puncak Jaya, their functional life as active glaciers is effectively over,” said Donaldi Permana, a climate scientist with the Indonesian Agency for Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics (BMKG).

Future projections suggest that the main glacial ice could disappear completely by around 2030, although BMKG estimates indicate an even earlier loss, potentially hastened by the current El Niño.  Past El Niño events have accelerated thinning: during 2015‑2016 the ice lost about 5.3 meters (17 feet) in a single year, and the 2023‑2024 El Niño saw a loss of 2 to 4 meters (7 to 13 feet) per year.  Ongoing satellite monitoring and the upcoming 2026 aerial survey will continue to track the final remnants of this tropical glacier.
summary: Puncak Jaya Glaciers Shrink to Tiny Fragments, Near Disappearance.

content: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 16 – NGC… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! NGC 7129: Star Formation with Jets from Webb Explanation: How do stars form? To help answer this question, NASA used the James Webb Space Telescope to take the featured detailed image of the star-forming region NGC 7129 in infrared light. Star formation progresses when gravity pulls together massive amounts of gas, but soon things can get complicated when previously formed stars emit powerful jets and winds — and some then explode. Opaque dust can form in the cool atmospheres of stars and, when dispersed, can obstruct visible-light images. Many stars can be seen to be forming in the featured image, with the young stars on the left, in the gold-colored gas, typically being more mature than the young stars on the right — in the red region. Studying stars at different stages of development bolsters understanding about what physical processes are most important and when.
